British Government's Response to the Home Rule Agitation

As the Home Rule Leagues expanded their activities, the colonial government became increasingly concerned about organised nationalist mobilisation.

Authorities used restrictions on public activity, press-related measures and action against political leaders to control the campaign.

Internment of Annie Besant in 1917

In June 1917, the Madras government placed Annie Besant and her associates B. P. Wadia and George Arundale under internment.

Internment meant that the government restricted their liberty and confined them without an ordinary criminal conviction for their political activities.

The action produced widespread protests. Political leaders and organisations that had not fully supported the Home Rule campaign also criticised the government's treatment of Besant.

The protests helped bring renewed attention to the demand for self-government.

The Montagu Declaration of 20 August 1917

On 20 August 1917, Edwin Samuel Montagu, the British Secretary of State for India, announced a statement of British government policy concerning India's constitutional development.

The declaration stated that British policy aimed at increasing Indian participation in administration and progressively developing self-governing institutions, with the eventual objective of responsible government in India as part of the British Empire.

Responsible Government

Responsible government is a system in which the executive is politically accountable to a representative legislature. In the parliamentary form of responsible government, the executive must retain the confidence of the elected legislative majority or the elected house.

The Montagu Declaration recognised responsible government as a long-term policy objective. It did not grant immediate Home Rule or establish a fully responsible Indian government in 1917.

The British government retained control over the pace and extent of constitutional change.

The declaration came during wartime, when nationalist demands and political pressure were increasing. The Home Rule agitation was an important part of this broader political setting.

Annie Besant Becomes Congress President

Following protests against her detention, Annie Besant was released in September 1917.

She subsequently presided over the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in December 1917.

She became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress.

This development demonstrated the political prominence she had acquired during the Home Rule agitation.

Why the Home Rule Movement Declined

The movement lost much of its earlier momentum during 1918 and the following period.

Several developments contributed to its decline:

  • The Montagu Declaration and subsequent reform proposals persuaded some Moderates to favour constitutional negotiations rather than continued agitation.
  • Political leaders disagreed about whether proposed British reforms were sufficient and how they should be treated.
  • Besant's position on some questions of political resistance and constitutional reform changed over time, making unified leadership more difficult.
  • Tilak spent an extended period in England pursuing a legal case, reducing his direct participation in organising the movement in India.
  • After the war, new political issues and methods of nationalist mobilisation increasingly attracted public attention.

The movement's decline did not mean that its political influence disappeared.

Importance in the Indian National Movement

Revival of Political Activity

The Home Rule Leagues helped revive organised nationalist political work during a period when the Congress had not been conducting sustained agitation throughout the year.

Popularisation of Self-Government

By repeatedly explaining the demand for Home Rule, the leagues helped establish self-government as an important objective of nationalist political discussion.

Development of Political Organisation

Local branches, public meetings and communication networks strengthened the experience of nationalist workers in political education and mobilisation.

Some of these workers and organisational connections contributed to later phases of the national movement.

Contribution to Political Cooperation

The Home Rule period encouraged cooperation between political groups that had previously remained divided.

The reunion of Congress factions and the Lucknow Pact of 1916 were important expressions of this trend.

Limits of the Achievement

Neither the Home Rule Leagues nor the Lucknow Pact immediately transferred governing power to Indians.

The pact represented agreement between political organisations on constitutional demands. The movement raised public awareness and strengthened mobilisation, but self-government remained a goal rather than an achieved constitutional reality.

The Congress–League agreement also did not permanently remove disagreements about political representation.

Distinctions That Connect the Major Developments

Home Rule Leagues and the Lucknow Pact: The leagues were organisations that mobilised support for self-government. The Lucknow Pact was an agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League on constitutional reform demands.

Congress reunion and Congress–League cooperation: The first concerned unity within the Congress. The second concerned cooperation between 2 separate political organisations.

1909 and 1916: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced under the 1909 reforms. In 1916, the Congress accepted separate electorates within the proposed Lucknow reform scheme.

1916 and 1917: The 1916 movement demanded Home Rule. The Montagu Declaration of 1917 announced gradual progress towards responsible government as British policy, without immediately granting it.

Home Rule and later mass nationalism: The Home Rule agitation helped expand nationalist political organisation before the major Gandhian mass movements beginning in 1919. It was an important preparatory phase, not a substitute for those later movements.

Prelims focus

  • June 1917: Annie Besant and her associates were interned.
  • 20 August 1917: Edwin Montagu announced the British policy of progressively developing responsible government in India.
  • September 1917: Annie Besant was released.
  • December 1917: Annie Besant became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress at Calcutta.
  • The Home Rule Movement helped revive nationalist activity, strengthen organisation and popularise the demand for self-government.
  • Trap: The Montagu Declaration announced a policy objective; it did not immediately establish responsible government or grant complete independence.
